items.title: Would You Upgrade Your Old Car’s Infotainment If It Cost You Almost Every Button?
items.summary:
These days, car owners broadly are hoping to see a touch fewer screens in their vehicles, and more traditional buttons. This isn’t anecdotal; many automakers have admitted to as much . But if you are one of the fortunate few to own a Bentley from about 10 years ago, you now have a unique opportunity: the choice to add a much larger, greatly improved touchscreen to your vehicle. All it’ll cost you is nearly every climate button and knob.

This week, Bentley announced a comprehensive infotainment upgrade for second-generation Continental GT and Flying Spur models, for an undisclosed price. These cars already had touchscreens from the factory, but they were the more antiquated kind, with poor precision, laggy behavior, and generally limited capabilities. These vehicles wouldn’t have had Apple CarPlay; Bentley didn’t add that in until the third-gen Continental and Spur in 2019. That’s a feature owners might like now.

The old screen was also small by modern standards, partly because an entire slate of buttons, dials, and a dedicated climate-control readout took up space below it. Those are things owners might also prefer but, if they opt for the new infotainment system, the bulk of them get ripped out, too. Even the CD player goes bye-bye.

The new, upgraded infotainment system at top, and the stock one below. Bentley 

Bentley says this new, 9.7-inch touchscreen boasts “impressively fast processor speeds” as well as “the latest navigation mapping.” It has a 2K (1440p) resolution and, naturally, supports wired and wireless phone projection. It’s got everything you’d want from…
items.t: Would You Upgrade Your Old Car’s Infotainment If It Cost You Almost Every Button?

items.title: This Rear-Engine, Flat-Six STI Is a Poor Man’s Porsche 911 Turbo
items.summary:
Ever dreamed of swapping a turbocharged Subaru boxer-four into a decrepit old Porsche just for the lulz? I know I have, and I’m certainly not alone. There are even kits out there to do it. But what if you want to live out your rear-engine Porsche fantasy without having to fork over Porsche money? That’s where Subaru’s flat-six comes in, and the crazy folks at Smeedia are hard at work putting an EG33 flat-six into the rear end of an STI. 

Oh, and did we mention that it’s turbocharged? Oh, yeah. This thing is going to be sick. This may be a “poor” man’s 911 Turbo, but there’s no shortage of custom fabrication going into this monster. Up front, where you’d normally find one of Subaru’s boxer-fours, instead there’s a fuel cell. The rear section of the chassis has already been tubed for increased rigidity (crucial with all the bits cut out of it), and the front will follow suit once they’ve sorted out some other aspects of the build. 

This isn’t Smeedia’s first attempt at an EG33 swap . In fact, one of these engines lived in the front of this very car (named “Blu”) for a while, and after throwing a whole bunch of boost at it, it needed a serious overhaul. Apparently, they bent two valves and warped the other 22 due to timing the engine incorrectly during the initial build. Expensive mistake, but the lesson has been learned. 

Their latest EG33 project will make their rear-engine dream a reality. The engine resides almost entirely in the STI’s trunk, and the exhaust is now mounted to custom brackets installed in the rear bumper crash bar. While the rear end had to be chopped…
items.t: This Rear-Engine, Flat-Six STI Is a Poor Man’s Porsche 911 Turbo

items.title: Race the Baja 1000 With Me via Livestream Right Now
items.summary:
The 2026 Baja 1000 is underway, running a big loop around the southern half of the Mexican peninsula that begins and ends in Cabo. I’m co-driving with a small team for a few sections in a tough little truck with some old and new friends as we prototype the next generation of BajaLite race trucks . We’ve got two vehicles competing, both equipped with satellite internet, beaming in-car footage for anyone who wants to get a taste of what it’s like to race the quintessential Baja truck: rear-drive, simple powerplant, small tires, and a whole lot of grit.

Check out my article contextualizing BajaLite to get a deeper download on what we’re doing here. But the short story is, my longtime friend Ron Stobaugh and his business partner John Slavic are spinning up a program called Desert Race Experience designed to get new people into the sport at a much lower cost than a Trophy Truck, but at a higher commitment level than a one-off, once-in-a-lifetime, arrive-and-drive vacation kind of deal.

This year we’re competing in Class 2—essentially an open, orphan category—as the BajaLite program gets dialed in. We’re racing to finish, flesh out team dynamics, and refine vehicle strategy. As long as satellite internet works, we should be live with an over-the-shoulder camera view on trackracecars.com , where you can actually pop in on a bunch of different competitors if you’re so inclined. I’ll be in car #2085, and our other vehicle is #2096. So if ours glitches, there will still be some action there. We should be off the starting line at about 11:30 a.m., PST, but schedules are dynamic in…

items.title: Toyota Tundra Recalled Again for Camshafts That May Snap While Driving
items.summary:
Toyota is planning a forthcoming voluntary safety recall for certain Tundra pickups ranging from model years 2022-2023 and 2025-2026. According to a leaked dealer notice sent to The Drive , some engines could suffer abrupt camshaft failure, resulting in a total loss of motive power. Concerningly, the memo specifies that improperly manufactured camshafts “could snap during driving.”

This recall covers approximately 62,000 vehicles. The affected camshafts supposedly came from one supplier, and an internal document specifies that they were localized in a single production lot. In total, Toyota estimates there to be about 300 affected camshafts, each fitted to cylinder bank one.

Importantly, this recall will not include any hybrid Tundra pickups or Sequoia SUVs equipped with the 3.4-liter, twin-turbo V6. It also does not include any 2024 model-year trucks.

Toyota will notify owners of involved vehicles by mid-January 2027. From there, those Tundra drivers should take their trucks to the dealer for a camshaft inspection to determine whether a replacement is needed. If one of their engine’s camshafts is from the affected lot, the dealer will install a new part for free.

This potential issue is not the first for Toyota’s V35A-FTS engine. Since the twin-turbo V6 launched in the 2022 Tundra, Toyota has battled problems with manufacturing debris adhering to the number one main bearing. Three expansive recalls stemmed from that issue, involving more than 270,000 vehicles . Toyota initially announced it would replace every V6 engine in trucks recalled for the aforementioned main…
items.t: Toyota Tundra Recalled Again for Camshafts That May Snap While Driving

items.title: The Ferrari Amalfi Is Proof Enthusiasts Don’t Understand Entry-Level Cars
items.summary:
“Oh, that was the slow Ferrari for women, right?” some middle-aged guy quickly said after I’d barely finished explaining that the 2027 Ferrari Amalfi I was refueling was the evolution of the California from the late aughts and early 2010s. If you know me, there’s no quicker way of pissing me off than putting someone or something in a box. Even though I wanted to abandon the conversation (and the gas pump), I responded: “Oh, how do you know—did you ever drive one?”

Of course he hadn’t, and neither have most people who look down on the least expensive and least powerful Ferrari, or the entry-level offering of any automaker. For what it’s worth, and as you’ll read in an upcoming review, I truly enjoyed the Amalfi. It’s about as usable as a Ferrari can get without losing that supercar edge that makes it thoroughly Italian. Plus, you can really explore its breadth of performance because it “only” has 631 horsepower.

Jerry Perez 

Interestingly enough, since driving it, I’ve told several people it might just be my favorite Ferrari; a comment that’s been met with gasps and follow-up questions. I’ve now driven every core model in the range (excluding the F80) and, in some cases, variants of each, and I found the Amalfi delightful. Yet, folks find it hard to believe that the lowest model can wow, or in some cases, be more likable than the one at the very top. I believe a combination of “more is better” and excellent marketing by car companies is to blame.

This applies to all cars in every segment, not just supercars. When it comes to off-roading, you’d be surprised how capable a…
items.t: The Ferrari Amalfi Is Proof Enthusiasts Don’t Understand Entry-Level Cars

items.title: 2026 Mazda 3 Manual Hatchback Review: Charmingly Basic; Questionably Premium
items.summary:
For eight years, I owned and drove the absolute snot out of a 2008.5 Mazdaspeed3. Metro grey, six-speed, sport seats, and tuned within an inch of its stock internals’ lives. The Racing Beat exhaust calmed the drone-prone factory note and added a hint of unequal-length-header rumble. On paper, the 2026 Mazda 3 has nothing in common with my old car, and yet, something about it just feels right .

The Basics 

The 3 isn’t new, and we’ve reviewed it plenty of times , but what stood out in my recent test drive is its humble transmission. It’s the last vestige of what Mazda once stood for (Zoom Zoom), and to its credit, it’s one of the few admirable holdouts for those of us who insist on shifting our own gears.

The six-speed is probably why driving this far more pedestrian hatchback feels oddly familiar to me. Just enough of that decade-old formula is still lurking beneath Mazda’s modern design and engineering philosophy that I can skip the orientation and get straight to the business of actually driving it.

I won’t wax poetic about manual gearboxes: either you get it, or you don’t. It’s not here because it’s the sporty choice or the frugal choice; it’s here simply because some people want the choice—and so far, enough people have raised their hands to keep it on the option sheet. For how long? It’s hard to say, but at least we can enjoy it while it lasts.

Byron Hurd 

Driving the 2026 Mazda 3

items.title: Scout’s Gas-Backed Traveler SUV Will Make 800 HP, Its CEO Told Us
items.summary:
Scout answered the skeptics on Thursday as it announced validation vehicles are now working through the shiny new assembly line in South Carolina. But even with early pre-production cars Scout still hasn’t disclosed a lot of the key specifications including the extended-range model’s horsepower. Until now.

On Thursday in South Carolina, Scout Motors President and CEO Scott Keogh told The Drive , “The specs of having something that’s 1,000 pound feet of torque, 800 horsepower, 500 miles of range, is a pretty phenomenal solution, and I think that’s why people are jumping there.”

Keogh was specifically speaking about the Harvester’s extended-range electric powertrain for the Traveler SUV. That 800 horsepower figure is the first time Scout’s made mention of horsepower.

To date, the automaker’s said the powertrain will have about 1,000 lb-ft of torque, do 0-60 mph in 3.5 seconds, and have 500 miles of total driving range. But horsepower was a missing link.

The extended-range electric powertrain, which will be known as the Harvester, will utilize a naturally aspirated four-cylinder engine from Mexico pulled from the VW Group’s parts bin. Which engine exactly has yet to be confirmed, but it’ll be retuned for generator duty cycles in the Scouts. Plans call for the engine to be mounted in the rear of the Scouts.

The electric 718 Boxster and Cayman are confirmed a-go . Sure—we’ll see more pure combustion and hybrid powertrains than the company probably would’ve anticipated earlier in the decade, but they don’t seem to be coming at the expense of the future. The 2026 Porsche Cayenne Electric is proof of that.

I don’t and can’t pretend to know how many buyers, especially here in the States, are lining up for a battery-powered large Porsche SUV. Policy changes, markets change, and who knows what the next five years will bring. That’s outside my scope. What I want to know is if Stuttgart has delivered the best big electric SUV it could, and I believe that, with a few rough edges, it has. And it’ll probably only get better.

Adam Ismail 

The Pros 

The greatest thing I can say about the Porsche Cayenne Electric is that it does indeed feel like a Porsche. It may not be as quick as other Porsches, and we’ll get to that in the other half of this review, but dynamically, there’s no question that it belongs in the family. That pin-sharp steering, the flat ride that neutralizes undulations, and the overall balance of comfort and poise are still world-class. And that’s all true of the standard two-chamber air suspension; the base model doesn’t even get Porsche Active Ride as an option.

items.title: Colorado Forced to Refund $1.1M in Speeding Tickets Thanks to Silly ‘Administrative Error’
items.summary:
Local governments nationwide have embraced automated, camera-based ticketing as a means of revenue generation traffic enforcement. Predictably, many of these roll-outs have gone pear-shaped in a hurry, either because municipalities have been overwhelmed by the sheer volume of infractions , or as in this case in Colorado, because automated systems have to rely on not-so-automated humans in order to function properly. 

Now the state has to refund more than $1 million in automated speeding tickets issued along a three-mile stretch of Interstate 25 outside Pueblo because somebody screwed up the paperwork.

The cameras were set up to catch speeders in a construction zone, pueblocounty.news reported . Violators were targeted in a corridor stretching from Indiana Avenue north to 13th Street . As the construction progressed, the work zone moved with it, with the mobile speed cameras following it. According to all involved, all speed limits were properly marked and violators were in fact exceeding those limits when they were issued tickets. At first blush, it sounds like a flawless pilot program. 

The problem? Nobody bothered to update the legal description of the work zone as it moved down the freeway. Because the locations of the violations didn’t match the filed paperwork describing the location of the work zones, all 27,000 of those tickets now have to be thrown out. 

If you received a violation notice, you can now safely toss it in the garbage, state officials said. If you already paid your ticket, a refund will be issued via snail mail with no extra effort required on your…
items.t: Colorado Forced to Refund $1.1M in Speeding Tickets Thanks to Silly ‘Administrative Error’

items.title: Scout Is Now Building Its Traveler SUV and Terra Truck in South Carolina
items.summary:
The term vaporware gets thrown around a lot. Just ask anyone that questioned whether the Tesla Cybertruck would actually ever get built. Ironically, it’s dying after a few years , but I digress, it did become real. Skepticism flowed when Volkswagen Group trotted out the Scout name and revived the Terra and Traveler badges for an electric truck and SUV. Timelines have slipped , but now, we have proof these things are getting built and are becoming real.

On Thursday in South Carolina, Scout announced it’s actually building validation vehicles with real stampings, initial welding, paint, and general operations underway at its shiny new factory. Looks like the iconic brand, and nameplates, will indeed return to the road.

Validation vehicles come long before pre-production models. These are test beds to work out production issues early in the game.

As you can see in the photo, the “concepts” that debuted the general design, look, and feel of these two vehicles are pretty darn close to what the finished product looks like. Scout didn’t provide close-up photos, but you can see the validation unit metal panels in the top left of the photos. They look familiar and like what we’ve seen to date.

Scout 

This is all taking place two and a half years after a ground breaking that took a pile of dirt and open land and turned it into a full-scale brand-new shiny factory. Scout said the construction is now entering its final phase with most the manufacturing equipment already in the factory.
